question:
For each natural smoothing order k, let S_k(p) be the actual polynomial (HermitePolynomial.sourceInterpolant k).eval p. To fix this family unambiguously, put t=p+1, a_{k,r}=sum_{m=0}^r binom(k+r-m,k)/m!, A_k(t)=sum_{r=0}^k a_{k,r}t^r, and S_k(p)=exp(-1)(1-t)^(k+1)A_k(t)+t^(k+1)A_k(1-t). Define f_k(p)=exp(p) for p<-1, S_k(p) for -1<=p<=0, and exp(-p) for p>0. Thus both S_k and f_k depend on k.

As in the predecessor, you may use the established endpoint jets: for every integer order 0<=j<=k, S_k^(j)(-1)=exp(-1) and S_k^(j)(0)=(-1)^j. No reproof of the coefficient or endpoint-jet construction is requested. Use the reusable finite-order gluing theorem: if real functions u,v are globally C^k and have equal derivatives through order k at c, then splice_c(u,v)(p), defined as u(p) for p<c and v(p) for p>=c, is globally C^k.

Fix k and prove f_k is globally C^k by applying this SAME theorem first at 0 and then at -1. Justify equality of all needed jets of the inner splice with S_k near -1 by local eventual equality, not merely equality at the single point. Prove that the nested right-valued splices equal the literal middle-inclusive f_k at every point, checking p=-1 and p=0 explicitly. State the conclusion with its quantifiers as forall k in N, f_k belongs to C^k(R).

Does this conclusion say that one fixed member f_{k0} is C^r for every r, or that one fixed polynomial splice is C-infinity? reference_answer:
Fix one natural k throughout the two gluing applications. Write R_k=splice_0(S_k,exp(-.)) and D_k=splice_{-1}(exp,R_k). The polynomial S_k and both exponentials are globally C^k. Their analytic derivatives at zero are S_k^(j)(0)=(-1)^j and (d^j/dp^j)exp(-p)|_0=(-1)^j exp(0)=(-1)^j for all j<=k. The first application of the finite-order gluing theorem therefore gives R_k in C^k(R). These are analytic jets: for a real polynomial, ordinary iterated derivatives of its evaluation agree with evaluation of iterated formal derivatives, as the source adapter proves.

For the second application, choose any open neighborhood of -1 lying strictly below0, for example(-3/2,-1/2). On every point of that neighborhood R_k(p)=S_k(p), since the inner splice takes its polynomial branch for p<0. Consequently R_k and S_k have the same derivatives of every order at -1 (germs/local eventual equality, not an inference from a single function value). In particular for j<=k, R_k^(j)(-1)=S_k^(j)(-1)=exp(-1). The j-th derivative of exp(p) at -1 is also exp(-1). Both exp and R_k are already C^k, so the second use of the same theorem yields D_k in C^k(R).

The gluing theorem includes its cut point. Its proof can be understood by induction on the finite order: for k=0, equal values and continuity of both branches give continuity across the cut; for a successor, equal values and first derivatives give a common difference-quotient limit at the cut, while neighborhoods away from it select one branch. The derivative is the splice of the branch derivatives, whose remaining jets agree through the lower order, so induction applies. This explains why the full jets, not merely the endpoint values, are consumed; no infinite-order premise has been added.

Identify D_k with the exact f_k. For p<-1, both equal exp(p). At p=-1, the OUTER splice takes R_k(-1), and -1<0 forces R_k(-1)=S_k(-1), just as f_k does. For -1<p<0, both equal S_k(p). At p=0, D_k takes the RIGHT exponential value exp(0)=1, whereas f_k takes the middle polynomial value S_k(0)=(-1)^0=1; this zeroth jet reconciles their different branch conventions. For p>0, both equal exp(-p). Thus D_k=f_k pointwise, including both junctions, and f_k is globally C^k.

Now quantify over the order used to CONSTRUCT the family: for every k in N, C^k(f_k). This is not forall r,C^r(f_{k0}) for a fixed k0, nor C-infinity of one fixed target. For k=0, a_{0,0}=1 and A_0=1, so the exact formula becomes S_0(p)=exp(-1)(1-(p+1))+(p+1)=1+(1-exp(-1))p. The literal f_0 has f_0(0)=1, is this linear polynomial immediately to the left of0, and is exp(-p) immediately to its right. Therefore its left derivative at0 is1-exp(-1)>0, whereas its right derivative is-1. They differ, so f_0 is not differentiable at0 and in particular is not C^1, despite being globally C^0 by the proved k=0 case. This canonical member refutes the stronger unindexed all-orders reading. It does not claim an exact maximal regularity formula for every other k.

All parameters and the two cuts are unchanged from the source target; strict positivity, grid sampling, normalization, ancillas and resource costs are not needed for this regularity proof.
